findings.claim: Flashcard answer: "Level 1 (L1) cache." (answer to "Which level of cache is the smallest and fastest?")
findings.truth: The computing fact is correct: L1 cache is the smallest and fastest. The concern is the literal string "Level 1", which sits on the checker's banned-string list. That ban exists to stop board band names leaking in; here it is ordinary cache terminology and must not be reworded, because "Level 1 cache" is the standard name. Flagged only so an automated banned-string sweep does not reject the whole unit on a false positive.

findings.claim: "ASCII, which uses 7 bits per character and can therefore represent 128 different characters"
findings.truth: True of ASCII itself, and the spec expects students to know character sets are limited by the bits available. The spec also states that binary representation of ASCII in the exam will use 8 bits. The lesson is already consistent with that: its worked text-file calculation uses 8-bit codes (200 x 8 = 1,600 bits) and it teaches that a byte stores one character. No edit needed; recorded so a future pass does not 'correct' the 7-bit statement, which is right.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/computer-science-J277.md 1.2.4 Data storage - Characters: 'Binary representation of ASCII in the exam will use 8 bits'

summary: No fixes required. Every base conversion, binary addition, shift, image and sound file size, and answer key in the unit was recomputed and is correct (156 = 10011100; 217 = 11011001 = D9; 53 + 22 = 01001011; 00010100 shifted left 2 = 01010000 = 80; 10011100 = 9C; 2F = 47; 8 x 200 x 300 = 480,000 bits = 60,000 bytes; 4 x 50 x 40 = 8,000 bits; 44,100 x 30 x 16 = 21,168,000 bits = 2,646,000 bytes ~ 2.6 MB). Register roles, RAM/ROM volatility, storage capacities (CD 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB, Blu-ray 25 GB), star and mesh properties, protocol roles, IPv4/IPv6 and MAC formats, OS-versus-utility classification and the three Acts with their years are all correct. Decimal storage prefixes match the spec, and the '1,024 is also accepted' remark matches the spec's own Alternatives note. All 72 practice tariffs are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 8 marks, which J277/01 allows; no wrong-paper or fabricated-examiner claims appear. The unit correctly omits the names of the four TCP/IP layers, which the spec lists as not required.
